newsitem.title: UK: Owen quits NatWest Markets in major overhaul.
newsitem.headline: Owen quits NatWest Markets in major overhaul.

text.p: Britain's NatWest Bank said on Monday its investment banking boss Martin Owen had quit amid a major overhaul of the business which was draining the group's profits.
NatWest's chief executive Derek Wanless said he had not fallen out with Owen and the decision that a change of leadership was needed had been taken by them both after lengthy discussions.
Shares in the bank ended the day down 43-1/2 pence at 753 after dropping to 776-1/2 right after the announcement, retreating from a high of 821 pence.
Owen's future has been under a cloud since late February when NatWest Markets disclosed it had sustained multi-million pound losses over a two-year period in its derivatives division.

Wanless blamed a significant fall in NatWest Markets' profits -- which will also hit the group's half-year results -- on the fall-out of the 90 million pounds ($147 million) interest rate options loss.
But Owen's departure also coincides with a major shift in focus by NatWest Markets, which had spent huge sums in its pursuit of becoming one of the top ten global investment banking firms.
The bank, and Wanless, have been under intense pressure from institutional investors to improve returns, with investment banking seen as a drain.
Wanless said he had never suggested NatWest Markets would be all things to all people and in its new guise it would still provide global expertise in particular areas, while pulling back from others.
An analyst at one European investment bank said Owen had been offered up as a "sacrificial lamb" by Wanless although he was not convinced this would satisfy shareholders' demands for improvement.
But Wanless denied this was the case. "As often happens with these things, it was something that we both agreed on," he told Reuters, adding Owen's departure package had not yet been finalised.
While analysts were not surprised by Owen's resignation, they were disappointed NatWest did not give greater detail of the proposed changes.

Wanless said the group would redeploy capital away from areas such as the loan market, where banks lend huge sums at increasingly tight margins, to areas such as wealth management which generate regular fee income without being capital intensive.

Analysts said it would be hard for NatWest Markets to make any disposals and Wanless stressed the importance of the recent acquisition of U.S. bond trading house Greenwich Capital and mergers and acquisitions boutique Gleacher to its future growth.
Owen has been head of the investment bank since 1992 and has masterminded, with Wanless's backing, a string of important acquisitions.
Wanless refused to rule out further acquisitions by NatWest, which has lagged rivals such as Lloyds TSB Group Plc which has concentrated on retail banking and steamed ahead of its competitors.
"We'd always be looking outside and if there was something that made sense financially then we would be interested," he said.
NatWest recently approached Abbey National Plc about a possible merger to increase its domestic retail lending.
Wanless said the group had a regular programme of talking to its shareholders and this would continue, but their discontent had been overstated.
He remains confident he can pull NatWest Markets out of difficulty and turn the fortunes of the group around. Asked if he would personally be the one to do this, he replied "That's my intention".

NatWest will not retreat entirely from investment banking but will refocus its efforts within the division, strengthening areas where it has a competitive advantage with a strong product or research base and high quality people.
It also disclosed the full impact of the interest rate options losses uncovered in February by warning profits for the whole group for the first half would not exceed 770 million pounds.
Wanless said this was the result of the knock-on effect of the options debacle, which had consumed enormous amounts of top management time and effort.

Banking analysts had expected a considerably better figure for the six months to the end of June, with one forecasting pre-tax profits in the region of 900 million pounds before the warning while others said they had already downgraded profits, with estimates of around 790 million pounds.

NatWest said the revision was entirely due to the problems at NatWest Markets, and said the continuing businesses of the group elsewhere were expected to show an improved first half performance compared with 1996.
Wanless said an independent probe into what went wrong in its interest rate options business was nearing completion, adding it had been a complex investigation and had thus taken time to complete.
The report has already been passed to the Bank of England and financial markets watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority, bankers said.
But Wanless declined to comment on what stage the report had reached or its likely outcome.
Five managers have been suspended as a result of the losses and millions of pounds in bonuses clawed back after the problems came to light.
($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
